help.display.title: Labels and display
help.display.what: Choose what labels show. Each view shows what it is about: interface names in L1, VLANs in L2, addresses in L3. What both ends of a link share is written once, in the middle.
help.display.why: Fewer, larger labels read better than many small ones. Turn a detail on here to show it in every view.
help.interfaces.title: Interfaces and modes
help.interfaces.what: Each row is a port. Its mode says what it carries: access carries one VLAN, untagged, for a PC or printer; trunk carries many VLANs, tagged, between switches; routed is an IP interface on a router or L3 switch.
help.interfaces.why: Both ends of a link must agree on mode and VLANs, or traffic is dropped. The Problems panel checks this for you.
help.learnMore: Learn more in the user guide
help.link.title: Links
help.link.what: A link is one cable or circuit between two interfaces. Its medium sets how it is drawn; bandwidth, label and circuit ID appear in the label in its middle.
help.link.why: Medium and speed tell readers what the physical network is; a circuit ID is what you quote to a provider.
help.problems.title: Problems
help.problems.what: LineWise checks the network as you draw: addresses, subnets, VLANs, trunks, speeds and more. Click a problem to select what it is about; many have a one-click fix.
help.problems.why: These are the mistakes that break a real network. Suppress a finding you accept; the reason is saved in the diagram.
help.routing.title: Routing annotations
help.routing.what: Notes about the routing a device runs, such as an OSPF area or a BGP AS number. They appear as badges in the network (L3) view.
help.routing.why: Readers see at a glance where each protocol runs. LineWise draws them; it does not check them.
help.subnets.title: Subnets and IPAM
help.subnets.what: A subnet is a block of addresses, such as 10.0.20.0/24. LineWise tracks which addresses are in use, the gateway and the VLAN each subnet belongs to.
help.subnets.why: Planning addresses here avoids duplicates and overlaps, and the next free address is always one click away.
help.zone.title: Zones
help.zone.what: A zone is a labeled area, such as a site, a building, a DMZ or a cloud VPC. Devices inside it move with it, and zones can nest.
help.zone.why: Zones show where things are and which security boundary they sit behind.

problems.title: Problems
rule.VAL-001.fix: Give one interface another address, or put the two in different VRFs if that is the design.
rule.VAL-001.title: Duplicate IP address
rule.VAL-001.why: Two interfaces with the same address in one VRF fight over it: traffic goes to whichever answers ARP last.
rule.VAL-002.fix: Readdress one end into the other's subnet, or use Point-to-point addressing on the link.
rule.VAL-002.title: Link endpoints in different subnets
rule.VAL-002.why: The ends of a routed link must share a subnet; otherwise neither can reach the other's address.
rule.VAL-003.fix: Correct the address or the prefix length in the interface table.
rule.VAL-003.title: Invalid interface address
rule.VAL-003.why: A malformed address, or a subnet's network or broadcast address, cannot be configured on an interface.
rule.VAL-004.fix: Shrink or move one of the subnets, or put it in another VRF.
rule.VAL-004.title: Overlapping subnets
rule.VAL-004.why: Overlapping subnets in one VRF make routing ambiguous, so some hosts become unreachable.
rule.VAL-005.fix: Move one link to a free interface, or bundle the links into a port-channel.
rule.VAL-005.title: Interface used by more than one link
rule.VAL-005.why: A physical interface takes one cable. Two links on it mean one of them is drawn on the wrong port.
rule.VAL-006.title: Duplicate hostname
rule.VAL-006.why: Hostnames identify devices in logs, monitoring and this diagram; two with one name are easy to mix up.
rule.VAL-007.fix: Set both ends to trunk, or both to access.
rule.VAL-007.title: Trunk on one end, access on the other
rule.VAL-007.why: A trunk sends tagged frames that an access port does not expect, so only the native VLAN gets through.
rule.VAL-008.fix: Set the same native VLAN on both ends of the trunk.
rule.VAL-008.title: Native VLAN mismatch
rule.VAL-008.why: Untagged frames land in a different VLAN on each side, which joins two VLANs by accident.
rule.VAL-009.fix: Make the allowed VLAN lists match on both ends.
rule.VAL-009.title: Allowed VLANs differ across a trunk
rule.VAL-009.why: A VLAN allowed on one end only is dropped at the other, so it works on one side of the link and not across it.
rule.VAL-010.fix: Set the same access VLAN on both ends.
rule.VAL-010.title: Access VLAN mismatch
rule.VAL-010.why: The two ends put the same cable in different VLANs, which joins two broadcast domains.
rule.VAL-011.fix: Set both ends to the same speed and duplex, or both to auto.
rule.VAL-011.title: Speed or duplex mismatch
rule.VAL-011.why: A speed or duplex mismatch gives a link that is up but slow and loses packets.
rule.VAL-012.fix: Give every member the same settings, or take the odd one out of the port-channel.
rule.VAL-012.title: Inconsistent port-channel members
rule.VAL-012.why: Members of a port-channel must match in speed, mode and VLANs, or the odd ones are suspended from the bundle.
rule.VAL-013.fix: Create the VLAN or VRF, or choose one that exists.
rule.VAL-013.title: Reference to a missing VLAN or VRF
rule.VAL-013.why: An interface refers to a VLAN or VRF that is not defined, so its configuration would not apply.
rule.VAL-014.fix: Set a gateway inside the subnet and give that address to a router or L3 switch interface.
rule.VAL-014.title: Gateway problem
rule.VAL-014.why: Hosts send traffic for other subnets to their gateway; a gateway outside the subnet, or one no device holds, leaves them cut off.
rule.VAL-015.fix: Use the same protocol, group and virtual IP on every member.
rule.VAL-015.title: FHRP group mismatch
rule.VAL-015.why: HSRP, VRRP and GLBP peers back each other up only when they share the protocol, the group number and the virtual IP.
rule.VAL-016.fix: Connect the device, or delete it if it is not part of the design.
rule.VAL-016.title: Device with no links
rule.VAL-016.why: A device with no links is often a leftover, or a link that was never drawn.
rule.VAL-017.fix: Draw the link, or remove the address.
rule.VAL-017.title: Addressed interface without a link
rule.VAL-017.why: An address on an interface without a link suggests a link missing from the diagram.
rule.VAL-018.fix: Plan a larger subnet, or move some hosts to another one.
rule.VAL-018.title: Subnet over 90% utilized
rule.VAL-018.why: A subnet that is almost full leaves little room for new hosts.
rule.VAL-019.fix: Add a management IP in the device's fields.
rule.VAL-019.title: Device missing management IP
rule.VAL-019.why: Without a management address the device cannot be reached for monitoring or configuration.
rule.VAL-020.fix: Move the link to interfaces of the same media, or change the medium if it was set wrong.
rule.VAL-020.title: Media mismatch
rule.VAL-020.why: One cable cannot join a copper port to a fiber port.

term.accessVlan: The one VLAN this port puts its traffic in. Both ends of a link should match.
term.allowedVlans: The VLANs this trunk carries, such as 10,20,30-40. Empty means all.
term.bandwidth: The link speed in Mb/s, shown in its middle label (10000 shows as 10G).
term.circuitId: The provider’s reference for a WAN circuit, which you quote when you call them.
term.duplex: Full duplex sends and receives at once. Both ends must match, or set both to auto.
term.fhrp: A first-hop redundancy group (HSRP, VRRP or GLBP): routers share one virtual gateway address.
term.interfaceNames: Short names (Gi1/0/1) keep labels compact; long names (GigabitEthernet1/0/1) are explicit.
term.labelTemplate: What each device’s label says, built from its fields.
term.media: Whether the port takes copper or fiber. A link must join two of the same.
term.medium: What the link is: copper, fiber, serial, wireless, a tunnel or a console cable.
term.mgmtIp: The address you reach the device on for SSH, monitoring or SNMP.
term.mode: Access: one VLAN, untagged. Trunk: many VLANs, tagged. Routed: an IP interface.
term.nativeVlan: Untagged traffic on a trunk is placed in this VLAN. Both ends must match.
term.speed: The port speed in Mb/s (1000 = 1G). Leave it empty for auto.
term.vip: The shared gateway address hosts use; it moves to the backup router if the active one fails.
